title: Earth is closest to the Sun in January
logline: Gus is sure summer means we're closer to the Sun. Vera shows him the orbit, then the tilt.
description: Earth is nearest the Sun in early January, in the middle of northern winter. Seasons come from the tilt of Earth's axis. Sources and simplifications in the pinned comment.

claims.text: Earth reaches perihelion, its closest point to the Sun, in early January (around January 2 to 5) and aphelion, its farthest, in early July.
claims.source: NASA Science, 'What Causes the Seasons?' (spaceplace.nasa.gov/seasons); US Naval Observatory, Earth's Seasons and Apsides table (aa.usno.navy.mil/data/EarthSeasons)

claims.text: Earth's orbit is nearly circular (eccentricity about 0.017); its distance from the Sun changes by only about 3% over the year.
claims.source: NASA Goddard, Earth Fact Sheet (nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/earthfact.html): perihelion 147.1 million km, aphelion 152.1 million km, eccentricity 0.0167

claims.text: Seasons are caused by the tilt of Earth's axis (about 23.4°): the hemisphere tilted toward the Sun gets more direct sunlight and longer days, so it has summer.
claims.source: NASA Science, 'What Causes the Seasons?' (spaceplace.nasa.gov/seasons); OpenStax, Astronomy 2e, §4.2 The Seasons

claims.text: The Southern Hemisphere (e.g. Australia) has summer in December to February, when the Northern Hemisphere has winter.

simplifications: The 'myth' orbit on screen is drawn far too oval on purpose; the real orbit (the second state) is nearly a circle.
The two globes are lit from screen angles to show which hemisphere leans toward the Sun; the Sun, sizes and distances are not to scale.
Distance has a small effect on sunlight (about 7% more in January than July), but the tilt wins by far.

lines.text: Summer's hot because we're closer to the Sun.
Here's the real orbit. Almost a circle.
It's the tilt. Whichever half leans toward the Sun gets summer.
Closer to a fire feels warmer. But Australia has summer in December.
Seasons come from the tilt, not the distance.
